The Seine River. France's second-longest river, flowing four hundred and eighty-five miles from Burgundy through Paris and Normandy to the English Channel. Paris's rise as a power depended on the Seine as a trade and defensive asset, and the river remains iconic in French culture and art.

The Seine flows through the heart of Paris, defining the city's geography in the most fundamental way. The Seine islands, Île de la Cité and Île Saint-Louis, were the original settlement cores around which Paris grew. Medieval Paris depended entirely on Seine commerce. Barges carried grain, wine, timber, and stone to and from the city. The river's bends and islands made Paris defensible. Control of Seine crossing points was critical to medieval warfare.

The Seine has been extensively depicted in Impressionist art, especially by Claude Monet, who painted the same scenes at different times of day and through different seasons. The river flows northwestward through Normandy and empties at Le Havre, a major Atlantic port connecting French inland waterways to global maritime trade. Paris's riverside districts developed as distinct cultural and intellectual zones, particularly the Left Bank and the Latin Quarter.

The Seine is absolutely inseparable from Paris's identity and history. The river shaped medieval and early modern French geography and power throughout French history. It flows through this historic Normandy region to the English Channel. Claude Monet obsessively painted the Seine's light and the changing moods of the water. Medieval cities like Paris, Rouen, and other Seine-valley cities were powered entirely by river commerce and depended on its waters for survival and prosperity.
